name: The Group Project
blurb: Five minutes to present, and one teammate has nothing but bigger and bigger excuses
title: The Group Project: Funny Skit Script for 4 Students
description: A 5-minute comedy skit script for 4 students: one teammate did nothing and the excuses keep getting bigger. Free to perform and film.
h1: The Group Project: a 5-Minute Comedy Skit Script for 4 Students
logline: Five minutes before their class presentation, three stressed students discover the fourth member of their group has done absolutely nothing. Every question gets a bigger, wilder excuse, until the clock is almost out and they have to decide whether to trust the one person who never does anything.
setting: A school corridor or the front of a classroom. Props: a laptop or a folder, note cards, a watch or phone, one tiny folded sheet of paper, a pen as the clicker.

roles.name: Maya
roles.note: Teen, any gender. The organiser. Calm on the outside, about to explode on the inside.

roles.name: Leo
roles.note: Teen, any gender. Did all the slides. Asks the logical questions nobody wants to answer.

roles.name: Sam
roles.note: Teen, any gender. Watches the clock and announces the time, which only makes it worse.

roles.name: Jo
roles.note: Teen, any gender. Did nothing. Totally relaxed. Secretly a brilliant talker.

script.scene: SCENE 1 – A classroom corridor, five minutes before a group presentation

script.action: MAYA paces with a stack of note cards. LEO holds a laptop open like a tray. SAM checks a wristwatch every few seconds.

script.say: Five minutes. We present in five minutes.
Four minutes and fifty seconds.
Slides one to eight are done. Slides nine to twelve are Jo's.
Where is Jo?

script.action: JO strolls in, calm, holding a single sheet of paper folded very small.

script.say: Team! Big day. How are we feeling?
Jo. Your slides.
About that. Funny story.
Four minutes and forty seconds.
My laptop did an update last night. A huge one. It updated so hard it deleted everything. My slides. My photos. My name. It now calls me "User Two".
You could have emailed us.
My email was on the laptop.
Your email is on the internet.
The internet was also on the laptop.

script.action: Maya breathes in through her nose. Sam pats her shoulder.

script.say: Fine. Plan B. Jo, just tell us what your slides said and we'll talk about it.
Perfect. So. My slides were about... the topic.
Which is?
The one we picked. Together. As a team.
"Great Inventions That Changed the World."
That one! Wow. What a topic.
Four minutes and ten seconds.
You had the printing press, Jo. Slides nine to twelve. The printing press.
Right. And I want you to know I printed it. On paper. Beautiful work.
Where is it?
That is the second funny story.

I was walking to school. Wind. Huge wind. The pages flew up, and a bird took one. Then a second bird took another one. I think they're building a nest with it. Somewhere out there, a family of birds knows everything about the printing press.
It's not windy today.
It was windy where I was.
You live across the road.
It's a very windy road.
What is the paper in your hand?

script.action: Jo looks at the tiny folded paper as if seeing it for the first time.

script.say: This? Nothing. Personal.

script.action: Maya takes it and unfolds it. And unfolds it. And unfolds it. It is still small. She reads.

script.say: "Printing press. Old. Good." That's it. That's all of it.
It's a summary.
Three minutes and thirty seconds.
Okay. Okay. Honest question, Jo. Did you do anything at all this week?

script.action: Pause. Jo looks at each of them. Then speaks with great seriousness.

script.say: I did do it. All of it. I just didn't do it here.
What does that mean?
Have you heard of parallel worlds? Somewhere, in another world, there is a Jo who finished four perfect slides. That Jo is presenting right now. That Jo is getting a gold star.
Can that Jo come here?
That Jo is very busy.
Three minutes.

script.action: Maya sits on the floor, defeated. Leo sits next to her. Sam stays standing, staring at the watch.

script.say: We are going to fail because of a bird, a wind, and a parallel world.
Hey. Hey. Listen. You've got eight great slides. Give me the clicker.
Why would we ever give you the clicker?
Because I can't do slides. But I can talk. I talked my way through this entire conversation. Didn't I?

script.action: The three of them look at each other. They can't argue with that.

script.say: Two minutes.
You open. Thirty seconds. Then you hand it to me. Thirty seconds, Jo.
Thirty seconds. Watch this.

script.action: Jo faces the audience as if they are the class. Big voice.

script.say: Imagine a world with no books. No posters. No menus. Nobody knows what's for lunch. Chaos. And then one invention changed all of that. Today, my brilliant team will show you how.

script.action: Silence. Maya, Leo and Sam stare. It was actually good.

script.say: That was good.
Why was that good?
I told you. Talking is my thing.

script.sfx: A phone buzzes. Sam reads it.

script.say: It's from the teacher. "Presentations are moved to tomorrow. Tonight, each member must send their own slides so I can see who did what."

script.action: Everyone slowly turns to look at Jo.

script.say: Tonight, Jo.
Your own slides.
Before midnight.

script.action: Jo nods, very serious. Takes the clicker. Puts it in a pocket. Backs away toward the exit.

script.say: Tonight. Absolutely. No problem at all.

script.action: At the door Jo stops and turns back.

script.say: Small thing. Does anyone know how long a laptop update takes?

script.action: Maya, Leo and Sam chase Jo off stage. Blackout.

ul: Play it across the front of the room as a corridor: Maya, Leo and Sam start centre, Jo enters from the side and stays a little apart, like someone who might leave at any time.
Keep Sam on one spot, glancing at the watch. Every time-call is a small drumbeat; the gap between calls shrinks as the panic grows.
The tiny paper is the best prop: fold a sheet many times so it takes Maya three or four unfolds and still ends up small.
For Jo's opening speech, Jo turns full front and addresses the real audience as the class. The other three freeze behind, mouths open.
Land the ending with the slow head-turn: all three look at Jo at the same moment, hold two seconds of silence, then Jo backs out and the chase starts on the last line.
Jo must believe every excuse. Never wink at the audience. The calmer Jo is, the funnier the excuses land.
Each excuse is bigger than the last: a technical problem, then nature, then the universe. Give each one more confidence and a slightly longer pause before it.
Maya's anger is quiet. Speaking slowly and politely is scarier and funnier than shouting.
Leo's short logical replies (It's not windy today, You live across the road) need a fast pace. Do not wait for laughs; let them overlap.
Jo's thirty-second speech has to be genuinely good. Rehearse it as if it is a real school speech, so the surprise is real.
Common mistake: rushing the final line. Jo stops at the door, turns, and asks the question innocently. Wait for the laugh before the chase.
Move it to an office: four colleagues, a client pitch in five minutes, and one co-worker whose report was eaten by a printer.
For a cast of five or six, add more hard-working teammates who each try a different way to make Jo confess, or a second slacker who backs up Jo's stories.
Different ending: the next morning, Jo arrives with four perfect slides and refuses to explain how. Part two begins with the other three investigating.

prompts.keyframe: Four teenagers in a school corridor, three stressed students holding a laptop, note cards and a watch, the fourth relaxed and smiling, holding a tiny folded paper, bright daylight from windows, wide shot, cinematic still, 16:9
shots: Medium shot, slow push in on a relaxed teenager explaining something with big hand gestures while three classmates stare in disbelief behind, school corridor, bright light, comedic mood
Close-up of hands unfolding a tiny folded sheet of paper again and again, it stays small, shallow focus, comedic timing
Wide shot, three students slowly turn their heads toward a fourth who backs away toward a door, then they chase after, playful energy

faq.q: Can we perform this skit at a school show or competition?
faq.a: Yes. The script is free under CC BY 4.0, so you can perform it, film it and post it, even on a monetised channel. Credit it as "Script: cv.cm" in the programme or the video description.

faq.q: How do we make it work with three people or with more people?
faq.a: For three, merge Sam into Leo and have Leo check the time. For five or six, add teammates who each try one new way to make Jo confess; give each one a single question so the pace stays fast.

faq.q: What should Jo's thirty-second speech be about if we change the topic?
faq.a: Replace the printing press with any project topic your class knows. Keep the shape: imagine a world without it, show the chaos, then promise the team will explain. It should sound like a real, strong opening.
